What it actually does: Makes b point to the same object as a (same memory).
Do a and b share data?: ✅ Yes, everything is shared. Changing b changes a.
When to use: When you want two names for the same data (e.g., passing to a function).

What it actually does: Creates a new outer container, but inner objects are still references to the originals.
Do a and b share data?: ⚠️ Partially: outer list is new, but nested mutable objects are shared.
When to use: Flat lists/dicts with only immutables (ints, strings), or when nested objects don’t need to be independent.

What it actually does: Creates a new outer container and recursively copies all nested objects.
Do a and b share data?: ❌ No, nothing is shared. Changing b never affects a.
When to use: Nested mutable structures (list of lists, dicts with list values, complex objects) where you need full independence.
